blocks.text: Challenging the Eurocentric narratives of art history, ‘Along the Color Line: Traces of a Transatlantic Modernism’ at Museum Ludwig reveals the overlooked contributions of Black artists to modernism and the cultural exchanges that shaped artistic expression across continents.
Whose histories have been excluded from the story of modern art?

Marking Museum Ludwig’s 50th anniversary, ‘Along the Color Line: Traces of a Transatlantic Modernism’ examines the artistic and intellectual exchanges between the Black diaspora and European modernism, challenging established narratives of twentieth-century art. Curated by Eboa Itondo, the exhibition brings together painting, sculpture, drawing, literature and music, tracing connections between the Harlem Renaissance, the Négritude movement and contemporary artistic practices.

Taking its title from the writings of W. E. B. Du Bois, the exhibition considers how Black artists navigated racism, colonialism and cultural displacement while developing new visual languages and forms of representation. Works by Mildred Thompson, Herbert Gentry and Iba Ndiaye illuminate transatlantic artistic networks, while James Gregory Atkinson’s archival practice connects historical experiences of Black communities in Germany with contemporary questions of identity and belonging. By confronting the historical absence of Black artists within European museum collections, ‘Along the Color Line ’ invites audiences to reconsider who shaped modernism, whose contributions have been overlooked and how art history might be understood through a more interconnected global perspective.
This exhibition is on view at Museum Ludwig in Cologne until 7 March 2027
